label: Riverside
rationale: The record Nat Adderley is remembered for, and the one that put the title tune into the standard repertoire: 'Work Song' was lyricised and covered the same year by Oscar Brown Jr. on 'sin & soul' and has been a vocal and instrumental standard ever since (S2). Reception consensus across independent listing traditions: the Penguin Guide to Jazz gives it 4 stars and calls it 'the real classic... laced with a funky blues feel but marked by some unexpectedly lyrical playing'; AllMusic gives 4.5 stars ('near-classic... Highly recommended', Scott Yanow); the Virgin Encyclopedia of 60s Music gives 4 stars ('a brilliant amalgam of the soul jazz') (S2). Session gravity is the second case: a January 1960 Riverside date that put Wes Montgomery on the same floor as Bobby Timmons, Sam Jones, Percy Heath and Louis Hayes, with the cornet-cello-guitar front line that makes the album's sound (S1, S3) — the exact personnel web the canon is built to trace. Lineage: the tune became a soul-jazz standard and the record is the reference point for the Adderley brothers' funk-blues wing already represented in the canon by the Cannonball quintet albums. Discovery value is high: a cold listener gets a hit-quality theme, a blues-soaked band and Montgomery comping behind a cornet instead of a horn section.

personnel_record.notes: Two sessions, both at Reeves Sound Studios, New York City: 25 and 27 January 1960 (S1, S2, S3, S4 agree on both dates and the room). TRACK-TO-DATE CONFLICT, preserved not resolved: S2 assigns tracks 2, 4, 5, 7 to 25 January and tracks 1, 3, 6, 8, 9 to 27 January; S5 assigns the exact complement — tracks 1, 6, 9 to 25 January and tracks 2-5 and 7-8 to 27 January. The two sources are mirror images, so one of them has the dates reversed and nothing in the record decides which; every track's session_date is therefore null and epistemic_track is 'unk' for that reason only. Per-track PERSONNEL is not in doubt: S2, S3 and S5 agree on who plays on which track. Instrument doublings (Sam Jones bass/cello, Keter Betts bass/cello) are recorded as separate performance rows with their own track lists, matching how the corpus stores doublers. Album durations differ slightly between S2 (4:15 etc., total 39:02 per S1) and S1's track listing.

ballot.case_for: Work Song makes a defining case for Nat Adderley as a leader: its signature composition became a standard, with Oscar Brown Jr. supplying lyrics that same year (S2). The cornet–guitar–pizzicato-cello textures distinguish it from routine hard-bop sessions, while Wes Montgomery, Bobby Timmons, Sam Jones, Percy Heath, Keter Betts and Louis Hayes give it exceptional session gravity (S1, S3). The Penguin Guide's 'real classic,' AllMusic's 'near-classic' and Virgin's four-star assessment establish broad retrospective esteem, though those judgments are reproduced through S2. Its memorable blues themes and intimate standard interpretations offer an unusually accessible introduction to the hard-bop/soul-jazz continuum.
ballot.case_against: The title composition's canonical standing does not automatically establish the entire LP as indispensable: the alternation between groove-centered ensemble pieces and stripped-down standards can sound less concentrated than the contemporary Cannonball quintet's live statements. The dossier establishes favorable reviews more securely than overwhelming canon-list consensus, with Rolling Stone's three-star assessment providing a modest counterweight (S2). Most reception evidence is mediated through Wikipedia, and the dossier offers limited documentation of album-level influence beyond the title tune's afterlife; strong personnel alone cannot settle that distinction.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John treat Work Song as a strong consensus-core candidate, distinguished by its ensemble sound and leader statement rather than by the title tune alone.
